learningObjective: Identify when unstructured or structured sparsity actually reduces wall-clock time on GPU, vs when it only reduces FLOP count.

canonicalClaims.claim: Unstructured sparsity typically requires very low density (well below 10%) before its FLOP savings overcome irregular indexing and imbalance overhead on GPU tensor-core hardware.
conditions: Target hardware is modern NVIDIA GPU with tensor cores.
Unstructured means arbitrary zero pattern requiring index metadata.
nonImplications: Does not imply sparsity is useless; structured sparsity works.
Does not imply the break-even density is fixed; it depends on dtype and kernel.

canonicalClaims.claim: For LLM decode (bandwidth-bound), sparse weight formats that reduce HBM traffic can give wall-clock speedup, but only if a matching sparse kernel exists for the dtype.
conditions: A sparse kernel supporting the format and dtype is available.
nonImplications: Does not imply FLOP-only savings translate to speedup.
Does not imply all sparse formats have kernels.

misconceptions.claim: Any sparsity >50% gives proportional speedup on modern GPUs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Only structured sparsity (e.g., 2:4) has hardware-native support; unstructured requires software indexing overhead.

misconceptions.claim: Hardware transparently skips zero tiles for any sparsity pattern.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Sparse tensor cores require the 2:4 structure metadata.

misconceptions.claim: FLOP reduction directly translates to latency reduction on decode.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Decode is bandwidth-bound; FLOP savings alone do not shorten wall time.

implementationFacts: 2:4 sparsity: within every group of 4 consecutive elements, at most 2 are nonzero; hardware performs the compressed multiply.
Block sparsity (16x16 or 32x32 blocks) is another practical format with corresponding kernels.
performanceScenarios: Weight-only quantization achieves bandwidth savings comparable to structured sparsity and is often easier to deploy.
